Selling What Nobody Has a Budget Line For

Playbooklowob research

By lowob · 6 August 2026 · Updated 16 November 2026 · 7-minute read · Strategy

When no budget line exists, you sell against the cost of what the buyer does today, through a category they already recognise, to the person who owns the pain. The category story is for investors. The evidence on lost deals supports this: Matthew Dixon and Ted McKenna's analysis of 2.5 million recorded sales conversations found 40% to 60% of lost deals ended in no decision. In emerging technology, the status quo is the competitor you lose to most.

The buyer has no budget, no title and no comparison set

In an established market, the buyer knows what they are shopping for. They have a budget line, a job title that owns it, and three vendors to compare. Emerging technology has none of that.

That changes the job. You are not winning a comparison. You are creating a purchase that did not exist in the plan. Every step of the sale has to answer a different question: not "why you" but "why spend at all".

Each audience needs one belief (see One truth, three audiences). In emerging tech the customer's belief is narrow and concrete. It is "this costs me money now and that can stop". Anything wider belongs in the investor deck.

The money for new technology does exist, but it moves quickly out of experimental pots. Andreessen Horowitz's 2025 survey of 100 enterprise CIOs found innovation budgets had fallen from about a quarter of AI model spend to 7%, as spend moved into centralised IT and business-unit budgets. Menlo Ventures' 2026 survey found new budgets funded 55% of incremental enterprise AI spend, with existing software budgets funding 22%. Both are investor surveys about AI, not every emerging category, but the pattern is the one that matters: once a technology proves a saving, an owner creates a permanent line for it. Until then, you are competing for money that is already allocated to the current way of doing things.

Position against the status quo, not against competitors

You do not have competitors in the usual sense. You have the current way of doing things. That is your real rival, and it is cheaper to describe than a category.

The research on indecision makes the point in numbers. Dixon and McKenna's work, published as The JOLT Effect, found 40% to 60% of lost deals ended in no decision rather than a loss to a rival, and that prospects showed some indecision in about nine in ten calls. Gartner's survey of 632 B2B buyers, published in May 2025, found 74% of buyer teams showed "unhealthy conflict" during the decision, and that groups reaching consensus were 2.5 times as likely to report a high-quality deal. A new category adds to both problems: nobody has a reference point, so every member of the group can hold a different one.

Write down what the status quo costs. Manual inspections and the people who do them. Downtime between failures. Compliance fines and the audit hours that precede them. Energy bought at the wrong time. Fraud losses and the checks that fail to catch them.

Then price your product against that number, not against a budget that does not exist. A buyer can approve a saving. They cannot approve a category. Our explainer on value-based pricing sets out how to price against the buyer's next best option.

Be specific about where the cost sits. "Inefficiency" is not a line item. "Four field engineers spending a day a week on site visits that a sensor could replace" is.

Status quo costWhere it sitsWho owns itEvidence to ask for
Labour on manual checksOperations headcountHead of operationsHours per week, loaded cost per hour
Unplanned downtimeMaintenance and lost outputPlant or service leadIncidents per year, cost per incident
Compliance effort and finesRisk and audit budgetCompliance or risk leadAudit hours, findings, penalties paid
Losses the current checks missFraud or write-off lineRisk or finance leadLoss rate and the sample it comes from

A buyer can approve a saving. They cannot approve a category.

Borrow a category to get the meeting, then expand

Buyers file new things under old names. Use that. If your agent infrastructure looks like workflow automation to a procurement team, let it get in the door as workflow automation. Our comparison of workflow automation and AI agents shows how close the two can look from the outside.

The borrowed category is a door, not a home. Once you are inside and the first use case is proven, you widen the frame. The sequence is: familiar name, narrow pilot, visible result, then the real story.

Founders resist this because the borrowed category undersells the product. That is fine. The first meeting does not need to understand you. It needs to happen.

StageWhat you call itWho hears it
First meetingThe nearest existing categoryProcurement, the budget holder
PilotA narrow problem with a cost attachedThe operational owner
ExpansionWhat it really isThe sponsor and the board

Sell to the person who feels the pain today

The visionary in the organisation will love your product. They will take every meeting. They rarely sign.

Find the person with a hard cost on their own budget: the head of operations with a maintenance bill, the risk lead with a loss number, the compliance manager with an audit deadline. They have a reason to act this quarter. The visionary has a reason to talk.

Use the visionary as a sponsor. Ask them to open the door to the owner of the cost. Then build the case for that owner, in their numbers, on their timeline. Gartner's consensus finding is the reason to do it in that order: the cost owner is the person who can turn a group of different opinions into one decision. Our explainer on the buying committee covers the other roles to map.

First customers are design partners (see Your first ten customers are design partners). Here the design partner must also be a cost owner, or the pilot never converts. The next part of this series, First customers in a market that doesn't exist yet, sets out how to choose them.

Product truth and the claims register for something new

The product truth still applies: one sentence about what the product does that is true today. For a new technology, the temptation is to write what it will do. Resist it.

The claims register is harder when references are few. Keep three columns: what we claim, what evidence supports it, who can verify it. Where the evidence is a lab result rather than a deployment, say so. Where the only reference is a pilot under NDA, record what you can share and what you cannot.

Buyers in new categories expect thin proof. They do not expect exaggeration. One overstated claim costs more than ten honest gaps.

Investor story versus customer story

The investor buys the category: why it will exist, how big it gets, why you win it. The customer buys a problem solved: this process, this quarter, this saving.

Keep them in separate documents with separate owners. When the customer story leaks into the investor deck, the raise looks small. When the investor story leaks into the sales deck, the buyer cannot find the number and the deal stalls.

This is one system, not three problems (see You don't have three problems). In emerging tech that means the two stories share a product truth and a claims register, and nothing else.

CheckDone when
Status quo costWritten down in the buyer's own numbers
CategoryA borrowed category gets the first meeting; the expansion story is ready for after the pilot
BuyerA named cost owner, not the visionary
Product truthDescribes what works today, not the roadmap
Claims registerEach claim marked as deployed, piloted or tested in lab
Two storiesInvestor story and customer story in separate documents

lowob takeaways

  • Position against the status quo. Price against what it costs, not against a budget that does not exist.
  • Expect to lose to no decision. Make the cost of waiting visible to every member of the buying group.
  • Sell to the cost owner. Use the visionary as a sponsor.
  • Keep two stories apart. Investor and customer stories in separate documents with separate owners.

Common questions

How do you sell a new technology when the customer has no budget for it?

Write down what the current way of doing things costs in the buyer's own numbers, then price the product against that. A buyer can approve a saving, not a category. Once the saving is proven, the owner can create a permanent budget line.

Why do so many B2B deals end in no decision?

Buyers stall when they fear making the wrong choice and when the buying group disagrees. Dixon and McKenna's analysis of 2.5 million sales calls found 40% to 60% of lost deals ended in no decision, and Gartner found 74% of buyer teams showed unhealthy conflict.

Who should I sell emerging tech to inside a large organisation?

The person with a hard cost on their own budget, such as a head of operations or risk lead. The visionary rarely signs, so use them to open the door.

Should a startup describe itself as a new category in sales meetings?

Not at first. Use the nearest existing category to get the meeting, prove a narrow pilot, then widen the frame to what the product really is.
